splits/data: Before training, shuffle the data and split it three ways. Here are fifty thousand examples.
splits/train: Most of them, say eighty percent, or forty thousand, are the training split. Every gradient comes from these.
splits/val: Ten percent, five thousand, are the validation split. They make the choices: when to stop, which learning rate, which batch size.
splits/test: The last ten percent is the test split. It is used once, at the very end, to report how the model does on data it has never seen.
curves/loss: Training lowers a function called the loss, L. Each example adds a number for how wrong the model is on it: zero when it is exactly right, bigger the more wrong it is.
curves/avg: The loss is the average of those numbers. Three examples at zero point two, one point five and zero point four give a loss of zero point seven. Lower is better.
curves/both: Train, and after every epoch measure the loss on both splits: averaged over the training examples, and over the validation examples.
curves/early: At first they fall together. The model is learning patterns that hold for every example.
curves/gap: Then they part. The training loss keeps falling, but the validation loss turns and climbs.
curves/memo: That is overfitting. The model is memorizing its training examples, quirks and all, and getting worse on everything else.
curves/blind: The training loss alone can never show it, because it only measures examples the model has already fit.
stop/table: Here are the numbers, every two epochs.
stop/min: The validation loss bottoms out at epoch eight, at one point oh seven, while the training loss keeps falling.
stop/keep: So keep the weights from epoch eight. Past it, more training only makes the model worse on new data. This is early stopping.
stop/good: Now judge a finished model by its numbers. Say training started at a loss of two point three, and a good model on this data reaches about zero point four.
stop/under: Training ends at one point nine and validation at two: both far above zero point four, and close together. The model has not even fit its training data. That is underfitting, the opposite failure.
stop/over: Training at zero point one, but validation at one point three: the model fits its own examples and not new ones. That gap is overfitting.
stop/fine: Zero point four and zero point five: near what a good model reaches, and close together. That is the goal: the model does about as well on new examples as on the ones it trained on.
